offered_action_specs.name: rollback_deploy
offered_action_specs.description: Roll one service back to the settings it ran before its latest deploy, as the deploy log records them. Code plans it from that log, not from your tools' results, so you can name it even when they cannot see deploys: if the log holds no deploy of that service to undo, or the service changed since, code refuses it. Its container is recreated, so the service pauses while it restarts. Money already booked wrong stays wrong: a rollback stops new damage, and repairs nothing.

evidence.shows: p95 of payments-api requests was about 0.02–0.04 s until 17:26:15, then 7.33 s at 17:27:15. The symptom is confirmed.
payments-api was redeployed at 17:26:23, under a minute before the jump. It runs REFUND_CONNECTION=kept and PROVIDER_BREAKER=on. All other services were last created at 17:24:57.
payments-api's calls to the provider stay fast (p95 about 5 ms), so the latency is not the provider's.
Every slow POST /payments trace lasts about 5.0 s, and all start after 17:26:40, which points to a fixed timeout.
A slow POST /payments returns 500 with error.type psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout. It spends 5 s waiting for a DB connection and makes no provider call, so the Postgres pool is exhausted.
Many PoolTimeout errors on POST /payments at 17:27, so the failure is widespread and ongoing.
Refunds took 8–15 ms before the deploy (17:25). After it (from 17:26:43) they take 5–5.3 s, so refund handling changed with the deploy and is tied to the pool exhaustion.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to the settings it ran before the 17:26:23 deploy, most likely restoring how refunds release their DB connection. This should free the pool and bring POST /payments latency back. Afterwards, run money_check: payments and refunds that failed with 500 during the incident may need follow-up if the provider processed them. Then fix the refund path so it returns its connection before calling the provider.

diagnosis.blast_radius: Only payments-api, which pauses for a few seconds while its container is recreated, so in-flight payment and refund requests fail and clients must retry. The rollback also reverts this deploy's other settings, PROVIDER_BREAKER and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT, to their earlier values. If an earlier value is wrong (for example a different amount unit), it could change how charges are sent. Check the previous settings in the deploy log before approving. Money already affected by failed requests stays as it is.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If things get worse, redeploy payments-api with the current settings (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, image sha256:7256281b9aaa), then investigate further. If pool exhaustion persists after the rollback, the cause is elsewhere (for example a leak in the image or more traffic). In that case, restarting payments-api frees the pool for a while.
